CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Vulnerable Baileys npm package present on disk (CVE-2026-48063) AIWeaponization Medium
Surfaces hosts where the Baileys WhatsApp library is installed under node_modules so an analyst can pivot version vs. the CVE-2026-48063 fixed bounds (< 6.7.22 on v6, < 7.0.0-rc12 on v7). Pure asset-inventory pivot — combine with a follow-up read of package.json to extract version. Rationale: GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg explicitly names affected packages 'baileys' and '@whiskeysockets/baileys' with fixed versions 6.7.22 and 7.0.0-rc12. package.json under those node_modules subpaths is the unambiguous on-disk artifact. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg, https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys (patch commit 3beb08e). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WhatsApp bot/chat server already patched to >=6.7.22 or >=7.0.0-rc12 (true positive on inventory, false positive on alert — must read version from package.json)
  • Developer workstation with a checked-out copy of the Baileys source repository for contribution work
  • CI/CD build agent that transiently materialises the package during npm install before publishing the artifact
  • Test/sandbox VM intentionally running an old Baileys to reproduce the vuln
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe", "npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "install"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — for each hit, read the package.json `version` field; if >=6.7.22 (v6) or >=7.0.0-rc12 (v7) close as not-vulnerable. Identify the owning service (systemd unit, PM2 process, container) and business owner. 2. CONTAIN — if vulnerable and exposed to untrusted WhatsApp peers, request the team upgrade via `npm i baileys@latest` / `@whiskeysockets/baileys@latest` or apply the workaround (drop messages.upsert events with requestId field, set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false). 3. HUNT — pivot to UC2 to find when the vulnerable version was installed and by whom; pivot to UC3/UC5 to check for in-the-wild exploitation against the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| where FolderPath endswith @"\node_modules\baileys" or FolderPath endswith @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count() by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| where TargetFilePath endswith @"\node_modules\baileys\package.json" or TargetFilePath endswith @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Vulnerable Baileys npm package on disk (CVE-2026-48063)

Baileys npm package install or upgrade activity AIDelivery Medium
Detects npm/yarn/pnpm/npx invocations installing or upgrading the Baileys WhatsApp library on managed hosts. Catches fresh introductions of the vulnerable code into dev/release pipelines and identifies who/when so the asset inventory in UC1 stays current. Rationale: Article explicitly names affected packages 'baileys' and '@whiskeysockets/baileys' and a versioned fix; detecting install/upgrade verbs gives temporal context (who introduced it, when) which is missing from a pure file-presence query. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineering team's intentional patch to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 (good — UC should fire so SOC confirms patch landed)
  • CI pipeline running `npm ci` on every build, generating recurring hits per build agent
  • Developer running `npm update` to refresh transitive deps without intending to touch Baileys
  • Renovate/Dependabot bot account performing scheduled upgrade PR commits
  • Docker build stage running on container build hosts
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and AccountName !in~ ("renovate-bot", "dependabot[bot]", "github-actions")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — read the full command line. Was it `npm install baileys@6.7.22` (good patch), `npm install baileys` (latest, ambiguous), or `npm install baileys@6.7.10` (introducing vuln)? Check user/account against approved engineering identities. 2. CONTAIN — if pinned to a vulnerable version on a non-build host, contact owner and request upgrade; if from an unknown account on a host that shouldn't run npm, isolate the host. 3. HUNT — within 24h before this event, look for the source of the command (CI job, shell session, IDE). After this event, run UC1 to confirm install completed and pivot to UC3/UC5 for any exploitation signs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe", "npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe", "npx.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "add", "update", "upgrade")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "add", "update", "upgrade")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe", "npx.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where CommandLine has_any ("install", "add", "update", "upgrade")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Baileys protocolMessage exploit signature: placeholderResendMessage + requestId AIExploitation High
Hunts for the post-exploitation artifact in Baileys application logs: a messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field together with handling of protocolMessage / placeholderResendMessage. This combination is the article's stated exploit chain for spoofing fake messages and history sync. Rationale: Article explicitly identifies the exploit primitive: 'malicious payload via the placeholderResendMessage' triggers a 'fake messages.upsert event' and the documented workaround is 'dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field' — confirming requestId is the high-fidelity differentiator. Defender/Falcon queries are process-pivots only since EDR does not capture WebSocket app payloads; the real detection lives in the Node app log stream (Sentinel Syslog, Splunk index, Datadog). Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesApplication logs (no CIM datamodel — raw Syslog/app)
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Verbose-debug logging that prints every messages.upsert payload, where benign upserts coincidentally co-mention protocolMessage in adjacent log lines within the same bucket
  • Test harness exercising the placeholderResendMessage feature against a controlled peer
  • Post-patch logs from a 6.7.22+ build where the field still appears but is now rejected by the library — confirm by checking for an accompanying rejection/drop log message
  • Self-chat / linked-device sync where the bot sees its own session protocolMessages legitimately
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "dropped" and SyslogMessage !has "rejected"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — read 30 log lines either side of the hit. Confirm requestId came from an inbound message (not bot's own outbound). Check the JID/sender of the upsert against the bot's known peers; an unknown / never-seen JID is a strong positive. 2. CONTAIN — apply the article's workaround immediately: drop messages.upsert events containing requestId and disable shouldSyncHistoryMessage. Plan a fast-follow upgrade to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 within 24h. 3. HUNT — for the same bot, look back 30 days for prior protocolMessage events from the same sender JID (this is the actor's exploitation window). Cross-check downstream actions: did the bot act on the spoofed messages (auto-replies, command execution, money transfer, etc.)?
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" or FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert"
| where SyslogMessage has "requestId"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("protocolMessage", "placeholderResendMessage")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nodejs OR baileys OR application) "messages.upsert" "requestId" ("protocolMessage" OR "placeholderResendMessage")
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/node\.exe$/i CommandLine=/baileys/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=baileys OR sourcetype=nodejs OR source=*baileys*) "messages.upsert" "requestId" ("protocolMessage" OR "placeholderResendMessage")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host source sourcetype
| sort - lastTime
Baileys app state sync integrity violation (corruption detection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects high-volume mutations of Baileys auth/state files (creds.json, app-state-sync-key-*, app-state-sync-version-*, baileys_auth_info/ folder) within a short window — the on-disk symptom of the article's 'app state sync jamming' attack where injected fake key shares corrupt the local state store. Rationale: Article states the exploit 'corrupt[s] the app state sync system by sending fake key shares' — and the workaround section admits 'no workarounds for the app state sync jamming.' Baileys' useMultiFileAuthState ships state to canonical files (creds.json, app-state-sync-key-*, app-state-sync-version-*) — bursts of mutations on these are the disk symptom of the attack. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg, Baileys source tree on https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys for the canonical state file names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial pairing / first-time QR scan where the bot writes every state file fresh (expect single burst on day one of deployment)
  • Normal linked-device re-key after WhatsApp force-rotates session keys (rare but legitimate)
  • Application crash + restart loop that re-reads/re-writes state on every relaunch
  • Backup job snapshotting the state directory by copying files in place
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" and FileChanges > 10 and not (Files has "creds.json" and array_length(Files) <= 2)
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — count the burst: >10 file changes/5m is suspicious. Compare the involved keys against a known-good snapshot (md5 of creds.json, list of app-state-sync-key-* files) if FIM baseline exists. Look at the spawning process tree to confirm it's the Baileys-using Node service. 2. CONTAIN — stop the Node service to halt further state corruption. Restore the state directory from the last known-good backup; if no backup, plan a fresh QR re-pair (will invalidate any attacker-injected keys). 3. HUNT — correlate against UC3 (protocolMessage exploit signature) on the same host within ±10 minutes — that confirms exploit chain. Look for outbound WhatsApp traffic from the bot to unexpected JIDs after the corruption (data leak / spoof reach).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed", "FileDeleted")
| where (FolderPath contains @"\baileys_auth_info\" or FolderPath contains @"\auth_info_baileys\" or FolderPath contains @"\baileys-store\")
   or FileName startswith "app-state-sync-key-"
   or FileName startswith "app-state-sync-version-"
   or FileName =~ "creds.json"
| summarize FileChanges=count(), Files=make_set(FileName, 50), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileChanges > 10
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath contains @"\baileys_auth_info\" or TargetFilePath contains @"\auth_info_baileys\" or TargetFilePath contains @"\baileys-store\")
   or TargetFileName startswith "app-state-sync-key-"
   or TargetFileName startswith "app-state-sync-version-"
   or TargetFileName =~ "creds.json"
| summarize FileChanges=count(), Files=make_set(TargetFileName, 50), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileChanges > 10
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*baileys_auth_info* OR *auth_info_baileys* OR *baileys-store* OR *app-state-sync-key-* OR *app-state-sync-version-* OR *\\creds.json)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(baileys_auth_info|auth_info_baileys|baileys-store|app-state-sync-key-|app-state-sync-version-|creds\.json)/i

Baileys fake-message-key / signature-verification failures in app logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for Signal-protocol verification errors logged by Baileys during message decryption — the symptom of the article's 'fake message key and payload' spoofing primitive. Bursts of these errors against a single peer JID strongly suggest active exploitation of CVE-2026-48063. Rationale: Article's core impact statement: the exploit 'allows anyone to spoof messages' via a 'fake message key and payload.' Signal-protocol verification phrases ('Bad MAC', 'signature verification failed', 'invalid message key') are the standard libsignal error messages Baileys logs to stderr when key/signature checks fail — the loud disk symptom of the spoofing primitive in flight. Defender/Falcon left empty: EDR doesn't ship Node app stderr. Cross-checked: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg, Baileys source for error-message strings. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesApplication logs (no CIM datamodel — raw Syslog/app)
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine WhatsApp protocol drift / WhatsApp-side key rotation causing legitimate one-off MAC failures (typically isolated, not bursty)
  • Bot restart mid-conversation losing session state and failing to decrypt in-flight messages
  • Out-of-order message delivery on poor mobile network where the local ratchet advances past a delayed message
  • Corrupted local state from disk error (pivot to UC4 to confirm)
  • Debug build with verbose protocol logging emitting these phrases on every successful decrypt-and-recover
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "recovered" and SyslogMessage !has "retry"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — bucket the hits by sender JID and minute. A single sender repeatedly failing verification (>3 fails in 5m) is the high-fidelity exploit signal; scattered single fails across many senders is more likely network/protocol drift. 2. CONTAIN — for any suspect sender JID, block at the application layer (drop messages from that JID) and apply the article workaround: drop messages.upsert with requestId, disable history sync. Upgrade to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12. 3. HUNT — pivot to UC4 (same host, ±10 min) to confirm app state corruption; pivot to UC3 to confirm placeholderResendMessage chain. Pull the offending sender JID's full message history with the bot — anything the bot acted on while in spoofed state is suspect output.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("signature verification failed", "invalid message key", "key mismatch", "MAC verification failed", "decryption failed", "Bad MAC")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nodejs OR baileys OR application) ("signature verification failed" OR "invalid message key" OR "MAC verification failed" OR "decryption failed" OR "Bad MAC")
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=baileys OR sourcetype=nodejs OR source=*baileys*) ("signature verification failed" OR "invalid message key" OR "key mismatch" OR "MAC verification failed" OR "decryption failed" OR "Bad MAC")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host source sourcetype
| sort - lastTime

Dev tooling beaconing to postmark-mcp / GlassWorm campaign infrastructure (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host-to-C2 callouts to the published Aikido IOC pack tied to the GlassWorm / postmark-mcp supply-chain compromise referenced in the article. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact IPs (142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255) and domains (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) the campaign uses for post-install exfil and second-stage download. Rationale: Direct match on the article's IOC pack: IPs 142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255 and domains giftshop.club, sfrclak.com tied to the GlassWorm / postmark-mcp supply-chain compromise. Any single hit on a corporate dev endpoint is a strong post-compromise indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/intel • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher / red-team detonating GlassWorm sample in an isolated lab forwarding telemetry to prod SIEM
  • Security tooling (passive DNS scanner, attack-surface monitoring service) actively resolving the domains for enrichment
  • Stale DNS cache on a host previously compromised but already remediated, replaying the resolution on TTL refresh
  • Sinkholed IP — if a takedown party now owns the IP, the destination is benign but the alert still fires
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseNdr.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") or RemoteIP in (BadIPs)
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull DeviceProcessEvents around Timestamp on DeviceName to identify InitiatingProcessFileName + parent chain — confirm whether the call originated from npm/node, Code.exe, an MCP server binary, or a browser extension host. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the device via MDE machine isolation; rotate any cloud / npm publish / SSH credentials present in the user profile (~/.npmrc, ~/.aws/, ~/.ssh/, ~/.gitconfig); revoke active session tokens for that user in Entra/Okta. 3. HUNT: Enumerate npm packages installed in the prior 24h (DeviceFileEvents on \node_modules\, package-lock.json writes) and any VS Code / Cursor extension installs (.vscode/extensions, .cursor/extensions) — fan out the same network query across the org to find peer infections.
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (BadIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (BadDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

VS Code / Cursor / node reaching Solana blockchain RPC endpoints (GlassWorm C2 channel) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts developer-tooling processes (Code.exe, Cursor.exe, node.exe, npm.exe) resolving or connecting to public Solana RPC infrastructure within a 5-minute window. The GlassWorm supply-chain attack referenced in the article uses Solana on-chain transactions as a resilient dead-drop C2 channel — a dev IDE talking to Solana RPC is rarely legitimate outside crypto-product teams. Rationale: GlassWorm (referenced by name in the article) is publicly documented to use Solana on-chain reads as a dead-drop C2 fetch — pinning the detection to dev IDEs and node runtime restricts the otherwise-noisy Solana DNS signal to the exact attack shape: a compromised VS Code/Cursor extension or npm postinstall script fetching its next-stage URL from a Solana transaction memo. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/ • https://blog.koi.security/ • https://www.aikido.dev/intel
ATT&CKT1102 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers working on crypto / Web3 product lines whose dev workflows legitimately call Solana RPC
  • Developers running local @solana/web3.js test suites or hardhat/anchor toolchain
  • VS Code extensions for Solana development (e.g. Solana Developer Tools) doing legitimate RPC calls
  • node-based browser preview / linter background process bundling a wallet SDK fixture
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("@solana/web3.js","@coral-xyz/anchor","--web3-test","hardhat")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Identify the parent of the dev-tool process — if it's electron/Code.exe spawned by a child extension host with --extension-id, capture the extension ID from CommandLine and check the marketplace for recent updates / takedowns. Inspect ~/.vscode/extensions and ~/.cursor/extensions for newly installed or recently updated packages. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the device. Revoke npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud creds in the user profile. Disable the suspect extension org-wide if a malicious extension ID is confirmed. 3. HUNT: Pivot on the extension ID across the fleet via DeviceFileEvents for the extension's manifest path; pivot on RemoteIP returned by the Solana DNS to find direct IP callouts that skipped DNS.

Execution or file write of known GlassWorm / postmark-mcp sample SHA1 hashes AIInstallation High
Direct hash IOC match on the three SHA1s shipped with the article: 2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca, d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71, 07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766. Covers both execution (process create) and on-disk landing (file write) so we catch drops that haven't run yet. Rationale: The article ships three SHA1 hashes tied to the campaign discussed (GlassWorm / postmark-mcp). Direct hash hits on workstation telemetry are the highest-confidence signal we can ship — any positive is investigation-worthy regardless of process context. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/ • https://bazaar.abuse.ch/ • https://www.aikido.dev/intel
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / malware analyst detonating one of these samples in a sandbox VM that ships telemetry to the production tenant
  • Threat-intel feed downloading samples to a designated analyst workstation for triage
  • Defender / Falcon sample-submission service caching the file in a quarantine path that still emits a FileWritten event
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a real developer workstation (not a malware-analysis VM). Pull DeviceProcessEvents within ±5 min of the hash hit to identify what wrote it (npm install? a VS Code extension install? a Slack file download?) and what subsequently spawned. 2. CONTAIN: Immediately isolate via MDE/Falcon; rotate ALL credentials present in the user profile — npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS access keys, SSH keys, GPG signing keys, cloud SSO refresh tokens. Force re-auth across SSO. 3. HUNT: Pivot on the source package name (if npm postinstall — check ~/.npm/_logs and the parent npm command) and search the org for the same package install. Check git push activity from this workstation in the last 7 days for unreviewed pushes — assume any commits/publishes since first hash sighting are tainted.

npm / node postinstall hook spawning network-capable LOLBin (supply-chain post-install execution) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the exact attack shape the article calls out: 'agent merges the PR, pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook, and touches production credentials.' Fires when node.exe / npm.exe is the parent of an interpreter or download utility executing a network-fetch command within seconds of an install. Covers the silent malicious-MCP-server-on-npm scenario referenced in the article (15 clean versions, backdoor on the 16th). Rationale: Article explicitly describes this attack chain ('the agent merges the PR, pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook, and touches production credentials') and references the September 2025 malicious-MCP-server-on-npm campaign. The parent (node/npm) + child (interpreter/download LOLBin) + cmdline-fetch-token triple is the precise behavioural shape of a malicious package postinstall. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/016/ • https://sigmahq.io/ • https://socket.dev/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate node-based build tools (electron-builder, node-gyp, prebuild-install) that download platform binaries during install
  • Husky / lint-staged git hooks invoking PowerShell to format files
  • CI agents on dev workstations running 'npm install' that fetch architecture-specific binaries via curl in their postinstall
  • Native module compilation flows (node-gyp → MSBuild) that shell out to download SDK headers
  • Cypress / Playwright postinstall downloading browser bundles via curl
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","prebuild-install","cypress install","playwright install","husky","lint-staged") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("electron-v","prebuilds/","cypress.zip","playwright-core")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull the full parent chain — InitiatingProcessParentFileName and one level up — to identify the npm invocation context. Extract the registry URL / package name from ~/.npm/_logs/*-debug.log around Timestamp and check the package on socket.dev or deps.dev for malicious indicators (recent maintainer change, sudden version bump from clean to backdoored). 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the device. Treat every credential on the workstation as compromised — rotate npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/GCP creds, SSH keys, cloud SSO sessions. If the package was published by an org-pinned maintainer, escalate to the registry security team for takedown. 3. HUNT: Org-wide search for the same package name + version across DeviceFileEvents on node_modules paths; for any other host that installed the same version, repeat steps 1–2. Pivot on the destination URL from the child cmdline to the GlassWorm / postmark-mcp IOC hunt (UC 1).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","Invoke-RestMethod","IEX","iwr","http://","https://","curl ","wget ","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","urlcache","bitsadmin /transfer","BITSADMIN")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentName = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where tolower(ParentName) in ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
| where tolower(ChildName) in ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","Invoke-RestMethod","IEX","iwr","http://","https://","curl ","wget ","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","urlcache","bitsadmin /transfer")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, ParentName, NewProcessName, ChildName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
